name: Murasaki Shikibu
info: Murasaki Shikibu (c. 973 – c. 1014 or 1025) was a Japanese novelist, poet and lady-in-waiting at the Heian imperial court, remembered as the author of The Tale of Genji, written in Japanese between about 1000 and 1012.

facts.born: c. 973 in Heian-kyō (Kyoto), into the northern Fujiwara clan; daughter of the scholar and minor official Fujiwara no Tametoki; her personal name is unknown, though she may have been Fujiwara no Kaoruko
facts.died: c. 1014 according to the date most scholars accept, perhaps when her father hurried back to Kyoto that year; Richard Bowring considers 1014 speculative and thinks she may have lived with Shōshi until as late as 1025
facts.role: Lady-in-waiting (nyōbō) to Empress Shōshi at the Heian court from about 1005 or 1006, serving as a companion-tutor for five or six years; author of The Tale of Genji, The Diary of Lady Murasaki and Poetic Memoirs
facts.known: The Tale of Genji, a novel of 54 chapters in Japanese; The Diary of Lady Murasaki; Poetic Memoirs, a collection of 128 poems; her fluency in Chinese, which she taught to Empress Shōshi in secret

t: Born into a learned but declining branch of the Fujiwara clan, Murasaki learned classical Chinese by listening to her brother's lessons, though Heian women were traditionally excluded from it.
She began The Tale of Genji while married or soon after her husband's death in 1001, and added scenes from court life after Fujiwara no Michinaga brought her to serve Empress Shōshi in about 1005.
Her diary, her poems and Genji are the main record of her life, and the dates of her death, c. 1014 or as late as 1025, remain disputed among scholars.
dyk: Murasaki Shikibu is a descriptive name, not a personal one: "Shikibu" refers to the Ministry of Ceremonials where her father worked, and "Murasaki" was most probably given to her at court after the character of that name in Genji.
ev: Born in Heian-kyō into the northern Fujiwara clan, in the household of her father Fujiwara no Tametoki
Travels with her father to Echizen Province, where he held a four-year governorship
Returns to Kyoto, probably in this year, to marry Fujiwara no Nobutaka
Her husband dies during a cholera epidemic
Enters the service of Empress Shōshi at the invitation of Fujiwara no Michinaga
Fujiwara no Kintō asks after the "Young Murasaki" at a court dinner, the likely origin of her name
Dies, according to the date most scholars accept; others suggest she lived to 1025

sections.early:
Murasaki Shikibu was born about 973 in Heian-kyō into the northern Fujiwara clan. The clan dominated court politics until the end of the 11th century by marrying its daughters into the imperial family and holding regencies, but her own branch had lost power. Her great-grandfather Fujiwara no Kanesuke had been in the top tier of the aristocracy, and by her birth the family stood at the middle to lower ranks, the level of provincial governors. It kept a reputation among the literati: Kanesuke had 56 poems in imperial anthologies, and her grandfather was a poet too. Her father, Fujiwara no Tametoki, attended the State Academy, became a respected scholar of Chinese classics and poetry, and entered public service around 968.

Her personal name is unknown. A court lady took a name from the rank or title of a male relative, so "Shikibu" refers to the Ministry of Ceremonials, where her father was a functionary. Her mother died, perhaps in childbirth, when Murasaki and her younger brother Nobunori were young, and she was raised in her father's household, unlike most children, who lived with their mothers.

Chinese was taught to her brother as preparation for government. In her diary she wrote that she listened to his lessons and understood passages he found hard, and that her father said, "What a pity she was not born a man!" She probably also learned music, calligraphy and Japanese poetry. She knew others thought her "pretentious, awkward, difficult to approach, prickly", and the scholar Thomas Inge believes she had "a forceful personality that seldom won her friends."
sections.rise:
Aristocratic Heian women lived secluded lives, and Murasaki's poetry shows limited contact with men other than her father and brother. Unlike most noblewomen of her status she did not marry at puberty but stayed in her father's household until her mid-twenties or perhaps her early thirties. In 996 she went with him to Echizen Province, a journey that could take as long as five days and was uncommon for a noblewoman. She returned to Kyoto, probably in 998, to marry Fujiwara no Nobutaka, a much older second cousin and a court bureaucrat at the Ministry of Ceremonials, who was in his late forties and had several households with an unknown number of wives and children.

Scholars read the marriage differently: Richard Bowring suggests it was harmonious, while Haruo Shirane finds resentment towards her husband in her poems. Their daughter Kenshi (Kataiko) was born in 999, and Nobutaka died two years later during a cholera epidemic. Murasaki wrote in her diary that she felt "depressed and confused" afterwards. She had read romances such as The Tale of the Bamboo Cutter, and scholars believe she may have begun The Tale of Genji before her husband's death. She circulated chapters to friends, who copied them and passed them on, and so gained a reputation as an author.

In her early to mid-thirties she became a lady-in-waiting, most likely because of that reputation. Michinaga brought her to court without following official channels. Bowring sees no evidence that she came as his concubine, while Chieko Mulhern thinks he wanted her to educate his daughter Shōshi.
sections.deeds:
Michinaga had sent his eldest daughter Shōshi to Emperor Ichijō's harem at about 12 and had her named Empress alongside Teishi, who already held the title; Donald Shively calls this unprecedented. Murasaki joined Shōshi's court in 1005 or 1006, when Shōshi was 16 to 19. Michinaga probably wanted skilled women around Shōshi to build a salon to rival that of his sister Senshi. Joshua Mostow believes he provided Murasaki as an equally or better educated woman to match the court of Teishi, whose lady-in-waiting Sei Shōnagon had written The Pillow Book. Shōnagon had left the scene when Teishi died in 1001, so the two writers did not meet.

Murasaki taught Shōshi Chinese, including the ballads of Bai Juyi, in secret and at odd moments, since written Chinese was considered men's language. Bowring calls it "almost subversive". Her diary, which covers about 1008 to 1010, records the ladies-in-waiting, Michinaga's temperament, the birth of Shōshi's two sons and the passing of new chapters of Genji to calligraphers for copying. She devoted half of it to the birth of the future Emperor Go-Ichijō.

Genji has 54 chapters and about 1100 pages and is thought to have taken a decade. She wrote it between about 1000 and 1012 and added scenes from court life while in service. Michinaga supplied costly paper and ink and calligraphers. She also left Poetic Memoirs, 128 poems arranged in a biographical sequence.
sections.opponents:
Murasaki's own diary records the friction around her. A lady-in-waiting who disliked her accused her of flaunting her Chinese learning and called her "The Lady of the Chronicles" (Nihongi no tsubone), after chapters of Genji were read aloud to the Emperor and a courtier remarked that the author was well educated. Murasaki replied in her diary: "How utterly ridiculous!" Mulhern believes she was flattered by the name. In Shōshi's salon there was hostility towards the Chinese language even though Shōshi studied it, and Murasaki publicly pretended not to know it.

She wrote disparagingly of rivals. Of Izumi Shikibu she wrote that "it does not seem to me that in herself she is really a poet at all", though Mulhern thinks her remarks were aimed at Izumi's behaviour and liaisons rather than her verse. Of Sei Shōnagon she wrote that she was "dreadfully conceited". Keene thinks Shōshi and her women may have shaped this impression, since Shōnagon had served Shōshi's rival empress.

Michinaga pursued her. Scholars such as Arthur Waley are certain she was romantically involved with him; her diary records a night when he came into her room and took a new chapter of Genji, and a poem telling him he had "neither read my book, nor won my love." Her flirtation with him is recorded as late as 1010, and his patronage was essential to her writing. She disliked the men at court, whom she thought drunken and stupid, and she appears to have disliked court life, calling Shōshi's court dull.
sections.last:
When Emperor Ichijō died in 1011, Shōshi retired from the Imperial Palace to a Fujiwara mansion in Biwa. Murasaki most likely went with her and is recorded there with Shōshi in 1013. A story holds that she retired to Ishiyama-dera at Lake Biwa to devote her last days to literature and religion. The temple shows the chamber where Genji was written, but Motoori refused to believe the story, and scholars dismiss the factual basis of her retreat; the story that she wrote Genji there on an August night while looking at the Moon is called a legend.

Her brother Nobunori died about 1011. Her father resigned his post and took vows at Miidera temple, where he died in 1029. He made a hasty return to Kyoto from his post in Echigo Province in 1014, possibly because of her death.

Scholars differ on when she died. Shirane says 1014 and a birth in 973 are generally accepted, which would make her 41. Bowring considers 1014 speculative and believes she may have lived with Shōshi until as late as 1025, and Waley agrees, since she may have attended ceremonies with Shōshi for Emperor Go-Ichijō around 1025. Her daughter entered court service in 1025 as a wet nurse to the future Emperor Go-Reizei, and went on to become a well-known poet as Daini no Sanmi.
sections.legacy:
Within a decade of its completion Genji had been distributed through the provinces; Emperor Ichijō had it read to him, and by 1021 all the chapters were known to be complete. Within a century it was regarded as a classic, and as early as the 12th century it was required reading for court poets and was studied by scholars who produced authoritative versions and criticism. Fujiwara no Teika published her poems in 1206. Edwin Reischauer writes that Genji, written in kana, "was the outstanding work of the period". Donald Keene calls it the "supreme work of Japanese fiction" and argues that she developed the monogatari form far beyond its bounds, while Shively sees as its themes "the tyranny of time and the inescapable sorrow of romantic love".

In 1673 Kumazawa Banzan argued that her writing was valuable for its sensitivity, and in the 17th century women were encouraged to read her books. Genji was copied and illustrated as early as a century after her death: the Genji Monogatari Emaki, a handscroll of the 12th century, is dated between 1110 and 1120. Artists such as Hiroshige, Kiyonaga and Utamaro illustrated editions, and ukiyo-e prints put the illustrations within reach of samurai and commoners. Dowry sets decorated with scenes from Genji were popular among noblewomen, and she was often painted at Ishiyama Temple, looking at the Moon.

Waley's translation was published in 1933, and reviewers compared Genji to Austen, Proust and Shakespeare. Kyoto held a year-long celebration of its thousandth anniversary in 2008.

summary: Murasaki Shikibu (c. 973 – c. 1014 or 1025) was a lady-in-waiting at the Heian court who, from a learned Fujiwara household, wrote The Tale of Genji, a diary and a collection of poems. Her husband died after about two years of marriage, and scholars still disagree about when she died.
